edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), Ad Scapulam, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Tamen (sicut supra diximus) doleamus necesse est, quod nulla civitas impune latura sit sanguinis nostri effusionem, sicut et sub Hilariano praeside, cum de areis sepulturarum nostrarum acclamassent: Areae non sint; areae ipsorum non fuerunt. Messes enim suas non egerunt. Caeterum et imbre anni praeteriti quid commeruerit genus humanum apparuit, cataclysmum scilicet et retro fuisse propter incredulitates et iniquitates hominum; et ignes qui super moenia Carthaginis proxime pependerunt per noctem, quid minati sint, sciunt qui viderunt; et pristina tonitrua quid sonaverunt, sciunt qui obduruerunt. Omnia haec signa sunt imminentis irae Dei, quam necesse est, quoquo modo possumus, ut et annuntiemus, et praedicemus, et deprecemur interim localem esse: universalem enim et supremam suo tempore sentient, qui exempla ejus aliter interpretantur. Nam et sol ille in conventu Uticensi, extincto pene lumine, adeo portentum fuit, ut non potuerit ex ordinario deliquio hoc pati, positus in suo hypsomate et domicilio. Habetis astrologos. Possumus aeque et exitus quorumdam praesidum tibi proponere, qui in fine vitae suae recordati sunt deliquisse, quod vexassent chritianos. Vigellius Saturninus qui primus hic gladiumin nos egit, lumina amisit. Claudius Lucius Herminianus in Cappadocia, cum indigne ferens uxorem suam ad hanc sectam transisse, christianos crudeliter tractasset, solusque in praetorio suo vastatus peste, cum vivus vermibus ebullisset: Nemo sciat, aiebat, ne gaudeant christiani. Postea cognito errore suo, quod tormentis quosdam a proposito suo excidere fecisset, pene christianus decessit. Caecilius Capella in illo exitu bysantino: Christiani gaudete, exclamavit. Sed et qui videntur sibi impune tulisse, venient in diem divini judicii. Tibi quoque optamus admonitionem solam fuisse, quod cum Adrimeticum Mavilum ad bestias damnasses, et statim haec vexatio subsecuta est, et nunc ex eadem caussa interpellatio sanguinis. Sed memento de caetero.
pass_a_gloss: Nevertheless (as we said above) it is necessary that we grieve, that no state will have borne with impunity the shedding of our blood, just as also under the governor Hilarian, when they cried out from our burial grounds: Let there not be burial grounds; their own burial grounds did not exist. For they did not reap their own harvests. Moreover, what the human race merited from the rain of the previous year has appeared, namely a flood and what was formerly, on account of the unbelief and injustices of men; and the fires which recently hung over the walls of Carthage by night, what they threatened, those who saw know; and the former thunderings, what they sounded, those who hardened know. All these are signs of the impending wrath of God, which it is necessary, however we can, that we both announce and preach and pray meanwhile that it be local: for they will feel the universal and supreme wrath at its own time, who interpret the examples of it otherwise. For even the sun, at the assembly of Utica, with its light almost extinguished, was such a portent, that it could not suffer this from its ordinary eclipse, placed in its own height and dwelling. You have astrologers. We can equally propose to you the outcomes of certain governors, who at the end of their life remembered that they had erred in vexing Christians. Vigellius Saturninus, who first wielded the sword against us here, lost his eyesight. Claudius Lucius Herminianus in Cappadocia, when, bearing it indignantly that his wife had passed over to this sect, had treated Christians cruelly, and alone in his praetorium was devastated by a pest, when he was alive and boiling with worms: Let no one know, he said, lest the Christians rejoice. Afterwards, having recognized his error, that he had made some fall away from their purpose through torments, he almost died a Christian. Caecilius Capella in that Byzantine outcome: Christians, rejoice, he exclaimed. But also those who seem to themselves to have borne with impunity, will come into the day of divine judgment. We also hope that for you this warning has been only a warning, that when you condemned Adrian and Mavilus to the beasts, and immediately this affliction followed, and now from the same cause an interruption of bloodshed. But remember for the future.

choices.english: For they did not reap their own harvests
rejected: For they did not drive out their own harvests
choices.why: correct translation of 'egerunt' in the context of harvests

pass_b_english: Nevertheless, as we said above, we are forced to grieve, because no state will get off scot-free for shedding our blood. Take what happened under the governor Hilarian: a crowd shouted from our burial grounds, "No more burial grounds!" but their own burial grounds never existed in the first place—they never reaped their own harvests. Moreover, the rain of the previous year has shown what the human race earned: a flood, a repeat of the ancient cataclysm brought on by the unbelief and injustices of men. And the fires that recently hung over the walls of Carthage by night—those who saw them know what they threatened. And the former thunderings—those who hardened themselves know what they sounded. All these are signs of God's impending wrath. We must, by every means possible, announce it, preach it, and pray in the meantime that it stays local; those who interpret these warnings otherwise will feel the universal and supreme wrath when its time comes. Even the sun at the assembly of Utica, its light nearly extinguished, was such a portent that it could not be explained by an ordinary eclipse, fixed as it was in its own height and dwelling. You have astrologers; ask them. We can also cite the fates of certain governors who, at the end of their lives, remembered they had erred by persecuting Christians. Vigellius Saturninus, the first to wield the sword against us here, lost his eyesight. Claudius Lucius Herminianus in Cappadocia, indignant that his wife had converted to this sect, treated Christians cruelly; he alone was devastated by a plague in his praetorium, boiling alive with worms. "Let no one know," he said, "lest the Christians rejoice." Afterwards, recognizing his error—that he had forced some to abandon their faith through torture—he died almost a Christian. Caecilius Capella, in that Byzantine end, exclaimed, "Christians, rejoice!" But those who seem to have escaped with impunity will face the day of divine judgment. We also hope this has been only a warning to you: when you condemned Adrian and Mavilus to the beasts, this affliction followed immediately, and now the bloodshed has stopped for the same reason. But remember this for the future.

review.notes: Pass B fails on the translation of 'interpellatio sanguinis' at the end of the paragraph. The Latin 'interpellatio sanguinis' (an interruption/calling to account of blood/bloodshed) is rendered in Pass B as 'the bloodshed has stopped', whereas Pass A correctly renders it as 'an interruption of bloodshed'. Furthermore, Pass B adds 'ask them' to 'You have astrologers' (Habetis astrologos), which is an addition not present in the Latin source.
reasons: Pass B adds 'ask them' to 'Habetis astrologos' which is not in the source.

Pass B translates 'interpellatio sanguinis' as 'the bloodshed has stopped', which is a significant shift in meaning from the Latin 'interpellatio' (interruption/challenge/calling to account) compared to Pass A's 'interruption of bloodshed'.
